METHODS FOR TESTING COTTON CORDAGES FOR RESISTANCE TO ATTACK BY MICRO-ORGANISMS

( First Revision )
0. FOREWORD
0.1 This
Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 14 February 1974, after the draft finalized by the Chemical Methods of Test Sectional Committee had been approved by the Textile Division Council.

0.2 This standard was first published in 1959 and now has been revised to make it up-to-date on the basis of the experience gained during its use. Cotton cordages are liable to deterioration by the action of micro-organisms. Since they are often stored, transported and used under conditions favourable for the growth of micro-organisms various protective treatments have been developed and their number is constantly increasing and hence the need for standard methods for testing the cordage for resistance to microbiological attack. 0.3 Three different accelerated mildew infection methods and a soil-burial method have been prescribed in this standard. The accelerated mildew infection methods are the humidity chamber method, the pure culture method and the mixed culture method. The humidity chamber method is intended for determining qualitatively the susceptibility of the cordage to the The pure growth of micro-organisms associated with attack on cellulose. culture method and the mixed culture method are intended for testing quantitatively the resistance of the cordage to fungal attack by infecting the cordage with micro-organisms capable of destroying cellulose. The soilburial method involves burial of the material in composted soil rich in The accelerated mildew infection methods prescribed in this micro-flora. standard are intended for evaluating the behaviour of cotton cordages under exposure to humid and warm atmosphere, whereas the soil-burial method is intended for assessing their behaviour under conditions of contact with damp soil for a long period. 0.4 Cultures be obtained of the organisms prescribed in this standard for the tests can from the Defence Research Laboratory ( Stores ), Post BOX 3

0.5 The methods prescribed in this standard can also be used for evaluating preservatives or treatments designed to protect cotton cordages from In such a case, the preservative or the treatdamage by micro-organisms. ment has to be applied to a uniformly good quality cotton cordage by the procedure recommended by the supplier or the originator and the treated cordage then tested. 1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard ( First Revision ) prescribes methods for evaluating cotton cordages for resistance to attack by micro-organisms based on accelerated mildew infection and soil-burial principles.

2.1 The test shall be carried out under the conditions laid down in resHowever, the ,specimen for breaking load testing pective test procedure. shall be conditioned and tested in the standard atmosphere for 65 f 2 percent relative humidity and 27 f 2�C temperature ( see also IS : 63591971*). When the specimens have been left in such an atmosphere for 24 hours in such a way as to expose, as far as possible, all portions of the specimens to the atmosphere, they shall be deemed to have reached moisture equilibrium.

Is I 1386- 1974 3. SAMPLING 3.1 Samples shall be drawn so as to be representative of the lot. Samples drawn in accordance with the material specification or as agreed to between the buyer and the seller shall be taken as representative of the lot. 3.2 From the sample selected take a sufficiently long piece ( see Note ) and mark to identify it as test sample.
NOTE- The length of the test sample should be sufficient for the number specimens required for 4.1.3.1,4.2.3.1 and 5.2.1.
of test

3.3 From the basic untreated cordage take a sufficiently long piece ( se6 Notes 1 and 2 ) and mark to identify it as the control sample.
NOTE 1 -If an authentic sample of the basic cordage is not available, a cordage similar in construction to the one under test should be used. The lenath of the control sample should be sufficient for the number of control specimens rcq&ed for 4.1.3.4, 4.2.3.2, 4.3.2 and 5.25. NOTE 2 - If it is known that the cordage under test had not been treated with a preservative, a sufficiently long piece from a good quality cotton cordage shall be taken, the circumference of which shall not vary by more than 20 percent of the circumference of the cordage under test.

SOIL-BURIAL
5.1 Test Soil METHOD

For the purpose of this method, prepare test soil in the manner prescribed in Appendix E.

5.2 Procedure
5.2.1 From the test sample, cut at random, 10 test specimens each 1.5 m long ( see Note under 4.2.3.1 ). Take five test specimens and test them as given in 4.2.3.1.

5.2.2

Take the remaining five test specimens.

5.2.3 Coil each specimen into a flat spiral (see Note ) and tie it with a thread so that it does not uncoil and yet a small length at the ends is free. Put the composted soil in five beakers of suitable size and bury one coiled specimen in each beaker so that the specimen is in a horizontal plane and is covered on all sides ( excepting the free ends ) with test soil 2.5 cm thick. Incubate the specimens at 30 f 2�C and at 98 f 2 percent relative humidity for 42 days. At the end of the period, remove the specimens, wash them free from soil and dry them in air. Condition them to moisture equilibrium in standard atmosphere and determine the breaking strength of each individual specimen by the method prescribed in Appendix B. Find the average of all the values.
NOTE- In the case of a strand of cordage, each specimen shall be wound around a wooden frame and secured by thread.

5.2.4 Leach the remaining five test specimens in the manner prescribed in Appendix D and test them in the manner prescribed in 5.2.3.

APPENDIX A ( Clauses 4.1.3.2 and 4.2.3.3
PREPARATION A-l. PREPARATION OF SPORE OF CULTURE MEDIUM

)

SUSPENSION*

A-l.1 Take about 250 g of potatoes, peel them off and cut them into slices. Weigh 200 g of the sliced potatoes, wash them in running tap water and place them in a beaker; add 500 ml of distilled water and keep the contents at boil for 30 minutes. Filter the hot extract through a thin layer of absorbent cotton previously wetted with distilled water. Preserve the filtrate. A-I.2 Take 25 g of agar and add 20 g of dextro$e and mix it with the filtrate (see A-l.1 ). Make up the volume to 1 000 ml with hot distilled water. Adjust the PH of the culture medium to 6.4. the temperatureof the culturemediumshouldbe kept NOTE- To avoidsolidification, above 45%. A-1.3 Put 5 ml of the culture medium into each of a number of 15 x 2 cm test-tubes and plug them with non-absorbent cotton-wool. In an autoclave, -terilize the culture medium with steam at a pressure of 1-l kg/cm2 for 20 minutes. At the end of the period, remove the test-tubes from the autoclave, place them in a slanting position and allow them to cool the culture medium to harden into `slants'. A-2. PREPARATION OF SUB-CULTURE

A-2.1 Inoculate the slants in the test-tubes with a well-sporulated culture of test organism [see 4.1.2, 4.2.2 (a) and 4.3.11 by means of a sterile needle. Incubate the slants for 7 days at 30 f 2�C. tne end of this period, a heavy growth of the freshly sporulatingtest NOTE -At
organism should be visible within the tubes. *If a miked suspension of aporcs of more than one test organism is to be prepared, suspenlions of spores of each test organism shall be prepared separately and the ruspensior, then mixed in equal volumes.

11

IS : 1386 - 1974 A-3. PREPARATION OF SPORE SUSPENSION

A-3.1 Add about 10 ml of sterile distilled water to the freshly sporulating sub-culture of the test organism ( see A-2 ) within the tubes. Bring the spores of the sub-culture into suspension by shaking or disturbing' them gently with a sterile glass rod. Filter the suspension through a sterile muslin Examine or similar fabric to remove particles of agar or fungal mycelium. a drop of the spore suspension under a low power microscope, and see whether 50 or more spores appear in the field.

APPENDIX

B and 5.2.3 )

( CZauses 4.2.3.1, 4.2.3.2,4.2.3.5
METHOD B-l. APPARATUS

FOR DETERMINATION OF BREAKING STRENGTH OF CORDAGE

B-l.1 A suitable constant-rate-of-traverse machine. B-2. METHOD

horizontal type of strength testing

B-2.1 Fix a iength of the cordage specimen in the jaws of the machine so that the distance between the jaws is 1 m. Operate the machine so that the moving jaw traverses at the rate of 150 mm per minute and note the breaking strength in kilograms.

STERILIZATION C-l. PROCEDURE IN METHYL

C
ALCOHOL VAPOW

C-l.1 Pack the specimens loosely methyl alcohol and keep them for ( about 27�C ). In the meantime, ing it with methyl alcohol vapour ature. Transfer the specimens

in a desiccator of suitable size containing 24 hours (or longer) at room temperature make another desiccator ready by sterilizfor a period of 12 hours at room temperfrom the first desiccator to the second 12

IS : 1386 - 1974 Connect the second desiccator to a desiccator with a pair of sterile tongs. water pump through a cotton wool filter and exhaust the desiccator at room temperature for 6 hours to remove traces of methyl alcohol. Bring the pressure in the desiccator to the atmospheric pressure by slowly letting in air through the cotton-wool filters.
